abstract: A compilation-cost predictor can be numerically correct for three different reasons: theorem, benchmark agreement, or accidental coverage by a compact regime classifier. We separate these certificate layers for a frozen shared-Tag TARE grammar. The initial forecaster F1(t) = min (C_R6L, C_D+, f_B) passes 102/102 prospectively staged rows but is exactly refuted on a fresh n = 3 instance: C_DP = 10 while F1 = 11. An existing all-n support theorem instead proves C_DP = C_D++ under the unit support-count objective, so F2(t) = C_D++(t) uses an independent support <= 2 evaluator without an unrestricted-DP call. It has zero error on 9,547 compared instances; the theorem supplies exactness and the panel checks implementation. An enlarged-borrow explanation B^() repairs the original row, but a hostile search finds 64 hybrid configurations outside it. A subsequent full 740-instance fibre census sharpens that negative: six of seven f_B^() fibres contain mixed exact costs, so the named vocabulary cannot provide an exact Psi-only explanation. The 64 selected hostile rows alone have a uniform offset only because selection conditioned on the gap. These explanation failures remain inside D++ and do not affect F2 cost exactness. The contribution is certificate separation: theorem-backed cost, refutable explanation, prospective and hostile evidence, and row-specific verification authority. No full-circuit, runtime, transfer, or hardware claim follows.
title: Theorem-Backed Static Cost Forecasting with Refutable Explanations for Quantum Compilation
